Background . Dengue virus (DENV) infection is the most common arboviral disease that affects tropical and subtropical regions. Based on the clinical hallmarks, the different severities of patients range from mild dengue fever (MDF) to severe dengue diseases (SDDs) and include dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. These are commonly associated with cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Principal Finding . In this study, we created an integrated and precise multiplex panel of cytokine/chemokine assays based on our literature analysis to monitor dengue CRS. A 24-plex panel of cytokines/chemokines was evaluated to measure the plasma levels of targeting factors in dengue patients with an MDF and SDD diagnosis without or with comorbidities. As identified in sixteen kinds of cytokines/chemokines, ten were significantly ( P < 0.05) (10/16) increased, one was significantly ( P < 0.01) (1/16) decreased, and five were potentially (5/16) altered in all dengue patients ( n = 30) in the acute phase of disease onset. Compared to MDF, the levels of IL-8 (CXCL-8) and IL-18 in SDD were markedly ( P < 0.05) increased, accompanied by positively increased IL-6 and TNF- α and decreased IFN- γ and RANTES. With comorbidities, SDD significantly ( P < 0.01) portrayed elevated IL-18 accompanied by increased IL-6 and decreased IFN- α 2 and IL-12. In addition, decreased platelets were significantly ( P < 0.05) associated with increased IL-18. Significance . These results demonstrate an efficient panel of dengue cytokine/chemokine assays used to explore the possible level of CRS during the acute phase of disease onset; also, we are the first to report the increase of IL-18 in severe dengue with comorbidity compared to severe dengue without comorbidity and mild dengue. Introduction Dengue virus (DENV) is the most prevalent arboviral disease in tropical and subtropical regions [ 1 ], which provides the ideal breeding ground for its primary vector, the Aedes mosquitoes. It is estimated that 100–400 million people in the world population are infected by DENV infection yearly [ 2 ]. DENV infection can be broadly classified according to the degree of severity into mild dengue fever (MDF) and severe dengue diseases (SDDs). The latter can be further distinguished into dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS), which encompass various symptoms such as circulatory failure or shock, multiorgan failure, and central nervous system (CNS) impairment, which needs intensive treatment and monitoring [ 3 , 4 ]. This condition exposes patients to a higher risk of death since no effective antiviral treatment is available for dengue infection, and the vaccine has inconsistent effectiveness against the four dengue serotypes [ 5 – 7 ]. Various factors influence the clinical course severity, including virus, host, and environmental factors [ 8 ]. The danger of dengue infection also building up in the secondary dengue infection patients as antibodies from the previous infection is being unable to neutralize the virus from heterologous infection, facilitating virus entrance to the Fc-presenting cell, causing higher viral replication and severe infection, known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) [ 9 – 13 ]. In addition, high virus titers can promote overactivation of the immune system and excessive secretion of proinflammatory cytokines, known as cytokine storms or cytokine release syndrome (CRS). This condition may contribute to various symptoms seen in dengue severity [ 14 – 16 ]. Some previous studies have shown that some cytokines are increased in response to severe dengue infection, such as TNF- α , MCP-1 (CCL-2), RANTES (CCL-5), IFN- γ , IP-10 (CXCL-10), IL-4, IL-6, IL-8 (CXCL-8), IL-10, and GM-CSF (CSF-2) [ 17 – 20 ]. Therefore, changes in the cytokine level might represent some specific event that determines the disease progression. For instance, viral protein nonstructural 1 (NS1) from DENV-infected cells [ 21 ] as well as an ADE infectious condition [ 22 ] can induce IL-10 production from monocytes. In DENV infection, IL-10 suppresses the DENV-specific T-cell response [ 23 ], supporting viral survival and replication and increasing disease severity. On the other hand, a low IFN- γ level correlates with a high viral load and more severe symptoms [ 24 ], indicating its essential role in early virus elimination and a better disease outcome. Despite all the previous research, no cytokine marker was approved to predict the severity of dengue. Based on previous observations, a twenty-four-cytokine panel was developed and confirmed using a dengue patient's plasma. We checked their level using a multiplex assay, along with the patient's clinical characteristics. The correlations between severity, clinical characteristics, and cytokine levels were analyzed accordingly.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Dengue virus (DENV) infection progression, including classification of dengue disease severity (mild dengue fever (MDF) to severe dengue diseases (SDD), with and without comorbidities), DENV infection diagnosis, and the development of Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS).
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Dengue infection can induce a Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) due to high virus titers causing overactivation of the immune system and excessive secretion of proinflammatory cytokines. Viral protein nonstructural 1 (NS1) from DENV-infected cells and antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) can induce IL-10 production, suppressing DENV-specific T-cell responses, thereby supporting viral survival, replication, and increasing disease severity. Conversely, low IFN-"gamma" levels correlate with high viral load and severe symptoms, highlighting its role in early virus elimination. NS1 can induce platelet activation, and activated platelets contain the IL-18 gene, leading to increased serum IL-18. Platelet activation also contributes to aggregation, endothelial adherence, and phagocytosis by macrophages, which promotes proinflammatory cytokine production. Macrophage cytokines facilitate B cell IgM and IgG production for dengue clearance. Progressive reduction of IgG may expose a risk to ADE in heterologous DENV infection, inducing more DENV replication in Fc"gamma"R-expressing cells and promoting proinflammatory cytokine secretion, including IL-18. IFN cytokines are protective against DENV replication, and lower levels in acute SDD suggest an inability of the immune response, promoting severe infection. The pattern of increased IL-18/IL-8/IL-6/TNF-"alpha" and decreased IFN-"gamma"/RANTES in acute SDD is implicated in severe dengue progression. Altered IL-18 and other cytokines in SDD+C are linked to comorbidity development. Negative correlations between platelets and NS1, and other cytokine interactions (e.g., IL-10 positively associated with TNF-"alpha", VEGF, IL-18, IL-1R"alpha", IL-17; IFN-"gamma" positively correlated with MCP-1, IL-12, IL-17, IL-1"beta", IL-2; IL-6 positively linked with IL-8, MIP-1"beta", IL-15, IL-18, MIG), suggest complex immunomodulation during dengue progression.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Levels of IL-8 (CXCL-8) and IL-18 were markedly increased in Severe Dengue Diseases (SDD) compared to Mild Dengue Fever (MDF). IL-18 was significantly more elevated in SDD patients with comorbidities (P < 0.01) compared to SDD without comorbidities and mild dengue, showing a steadily significant increase across all severity groups, especially in comorbid groups. Significant increases in IL-8, IL-18, IL-6, and TNF-"alpha" were observed in SDD compared to MDF, although TNF-"alpha" showed higher levels in MDF than DHF in one comparison. WBC counts were highest in SDD+C (acute phase), lower in SDD-C than MDF (acute), and lowest in MDF then SDD-C (convalescent). Platelet counts peaked in MDF (acute phase) and decreased with disease progression to severe, but increased in the severe group (convalescent) exceeding MDF. NS1 levels were lowest in MDF (acute) and peaked in SDD-C (slightly higher than SDD+C). IFN cytokines (IFN-"alpha"2, IFN-"gamma") and antivirus-associated factors (IL-12, MCP-1, RANTES) were generally lower in acute SDD than MDF. IL-7, IL-8, IL-6, IL-10, IL-18, MIG, MIP-1"alpha", MIP-1"beta", TNF-"alpha", VEGF increased prominently in acute SDD+C. SDD+C vs. SDD-C showed increased trends for IL-10, IL-6, TNF-"alpha", IL-8, IL-4, MIP-1"beta", VEGF, IL-18, and decreased trends for IFN-"gamma", IP-10, IFN-"alpha"2, IL-13, IL-1"beta", IL-2. Hospital time and ICU duration significantly increased with dengue severity (P < 0.001). The prevalence of comorbidities like diabetes mellitus and hypertension also strongly correlated with increasing severity (P < 0.001), with higher incidence in SDD+C compared to MDF.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The increase of IL-18 in severe dengue with comorbidity is a novel finding reported for the first time, distinguishing it from severe dengue without comorbidity and mild dengue. IL-18 was specifically identified as a cytokine that steadily and significantly increased across all dengue severity groups, with the most severe increases observed in patients with comorbidities, suggesting it could serve as a severity measure, particularly in comorbid dengue cases. Dengue IgG was identified as a potential marker for secondary dengue infection, suggesting specificity for classifying infection history. Hematocrit changes were not influenced by dengue severity. Increased IL-18 and IL-8, probable increased IL-6 and TNF-"alpha", along with decreased IFN-"gamma" and RANTES, are specific to acute SDD patients and severe dengue progression. The study's inclusion criteria aimed to ensure dengue-specific findings by excluding non-dengue infections and coinfections.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Adult dengue patients (mean age 61.6 years) in tropical and subtropical regions, in the acute phase of disease onset, categorized as Mild Dengue Fever (MDF), Severe Dengue Diseases (SDD) with or without comorbidities (SDD-C, SDD+C), and healthy controls. Specific focus on older people and individuals with chronic underlying diseases like Diabetes Mellitus (DM) and hypertension.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: IL-18 is a potential biomarker for predicting severe dengue disease progression, which is critical given the high risk of death due to the lack of effective antiviral treatment and inconsistent vaccine effectiveness. Findings contribute to understanding and managing Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) in dengue. The correlations with hospital time and ICU duration highlight the importance of medical care in severe dengue infection. Comorbidities like diabetes and hypertension are linked to increased severity. Progression from mild dengue to severe dengue, development of severe thrombocytopenia, increased NS1 toxemia, and immune response inability against DENV infection are significant health implications. These findings contribute to the classification and differentiation of dengue disease severity and diagnosis of DENV infection.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Age is weakly correlated with dengue severity (P = 0.01). Hospital time, ICU duration, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension are strongly correlated with increased dengue severity (P < 0.001), classifying them as indicators of adverse risk and worse outcomes. Dengue IgG is a potential marker for secondary dengue infection, which can be associated with higher risk of severe disease. Lower IFN levels indicate immune response inability, promoting severe infection. Increased IL-7, IL-8, IL-6, IL-10, IL-18, MIG, MIP-1"alpha", MIP-1"beta", TNF-"alpha", VEGF are potential markers for dengue severity and diagnostic utility for predicting adverse risk. Increased IL-18 and IL-8, with decreased IFN-"gamma" and RANTES, are involved in severe dengue progression. Altered IL-18 and other cytokines in SDD+C are associated with comorbidities. Severe thrombocytopenia and increased NS1 toxemia are observed in acute SDD.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: A 24-plex panel of cytokine/chemokine assays was developed and evaluated as an efficient panel to explore the possible level of Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) during the acute phase of disease onset. The study utilized bead-based multiplex assays (Luminex technology) with commercial and customized panels, incorporating quality controls (QCs) to ensure assay performance and pipetting quality. The selection of the top 24 cytokines/chemokines, including 6 biomarkers reported in over 10 papers, was based on a rigorous literature review of 45 articles, indicating their established relevance and reliability in the field. Several cytokines (e.g., IL-7, IL-8, IL-6, IL-10, IL-18, MIG, MIP-1"alpha", MIP-1"beta", TNF-"alpha", VEGF) are identified as potential markers for severity in dengue patients, suggesting their utility, supported by significant statistical correlations and differences (P-values reported). However, no cytokine marker was previously approved to predict the severity of dengue. The study acknowledges limitations, including a small sample size that may have hampered precision, and gender differences were not evaluated. The detailed mechanism by which IL-18 contributes to disease severity (exacerbating or preventing) remains unclear and requires further investigation. IL-18 is presented as a plausible option for a dengue severity measure due to its consistent significant increase.
recommended_alternatives: Dengue IgG (as a potential marker for secondary dengue infection)
